questions.q: In "Who needs this, and who is your first user Understand", which of these is a key idea?
o: Write a half-page idea: who, what you will do, what success looks like in numbers.
Write a short message you could send to a relative who is tempted by an advert: what to ask and who to see first.
Score: three adverts, 4, 5 and 2 red flags out of 5.
Review 3 adverts against your red-flag list and score each.

questions.q: In "Kick-off circle Understand", which of these is a key idea?
o: The mentor agrees the evidence you will produce in this course (listed at the end of each lesson).
Summary: some blood-related uses are established; many other uses are experimental; some adverts have no evidence.
Make a red-flag list for adverts: miracle language, no trial data, high fees, testimonials in place of evidence.
Write a 90-day next-step plan: what to do, where, how much, what to learn next. Pick a follow-on course from the catalogue.

questions.q: In "Start the practice task Apply", which of these is a key idea?
o: Evidence quality: a stronger study has a comparison group, enough people, results shared in a journal and repeated by others. A single story is not evidence.
Write a one-page summary: proven uses, experimental uses, uses with no evidence.
Present your red-flag scores.
Regulation: treatments need testing in controlled trials and approval before routine sale. Unapproved treatments can be harmful and expensive.

questions.q: In "Short modules Apply", which of these is a key idea?
o: Questions before any treatment: Is it approved here? Where is the trial data? Who regulates this?
Ethics: informed consent, honest information, fair access, and respect for the source of any cells.
Review 3 adverts against your red-flag list and score each.
Write three lessons learned and one decision: scale, change or stop.

Write a one-page summary: proven uses, experimental uses, uses with no evidence.
